title: The URL shortener project
idea: The project is a REST API, a server called over HTTP. Users sign up, log in and save long URLs under short codes. Visitors follow short links.
points: Six routes do the product's work: signup, login, shorten, redirect, list and delete.
Login returns a JWT, a signed token. Routes that need a user check it.
Each code has one owner, and only the owner can list or delete it.
You build it layer by layer: server, database, accounts, then URLs.

messages.label: POST /auth/signup
messages.note: An owner signs up with an email and a password.

messages.label: 201 { user }
messages.note: The API stores a password hash and returns the new user's id and email.

messages.label: POST /auth/login
messages.note: Later the owner logs in with the same email and password.

messages.label: 200 { token }
messages.note: A JWT comes back. The owner sends it with every request that needs a user.

messages.label: POST /shorten
messages.note: The owner sends a long URL, with `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.

messages.label: 201 { shortCode }
messages.note: The API saves the URL under a random seven-character code and returns the code.

messages.label: GET /:shortCode
messages.note: A visitor opens the short link. No token is needed.

messages.label: 302 to the long URL
messages.note: The API looks the code up and redirects the browser to the saved URL.

messages.label: DELETE /codes/:id
messages.note: The owner deletes the link. The token tells the API who is asking.

messages.label: 204 No Content
messages.note: The owner owns that link, so it is deleted. Another user's token would get 403.

code.title: Final project layout
code.caption: The finished layout. Each file arrives in its own lesson, so nothing here runs yet.

walk.text: Root files: dependencies, Drizzle's command-line settings, and your settings and secrets in `.env`.
`server.js` listens on a port. `app.js` builds the Express app and mounts the routers.
`db/` holds the Drizzle client and the table definitions.
`routes/` map each method and URL to a controller function.
`controllers/` read the request, call a service and choose the status code.
`services/` hold the rules and the queries. They know nothing about HTTP.
`middleware/`, `utils/` and `validation/` hold the auth check, JWT helpers and Zod schemas.

pitfalls: Follow the lessons in order. Later snippets assume the files earlier ones created.
Run each snippet before moving on. A broken step is easiest to fix right away.

quiz.q: Which request works without a token?
quiz.why: A visitor follows a short link without an account, so the redirect route is public. The other three need a logged-in user.

takeaway: Anyone can follow a short link; only the owner can list or delete it.

starters: Why does opening a short link need no login?
Why build this with Postgres and not MongoDB?
What stops one user from deleting another user's link?
